extracted.intended_audience: students, practitioners, and general readers interested in U.S. First Amendment/free-speech law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply legal tests used by U.S. courts to decide when government may limit speech under the First Amendment, including historical and modern standards and key case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and present danger test
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the words used 'are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about the substantive evils that the United States Congress has a right to prevent.' (Holmes, Schenck v. United States, 1919).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate 'proximity and degree' of the harm: ask if, in the circumstances, the speech is likely and near enough in time and effect to produce the substantive evil. Holmes framed this especially in wartime, noting that many utterances during war may not be protected because they hinder the nation's effort. Examples: Schenck (anti-draft advocacy). The test was intended to refine (not replace) the bad tendency test and was invoked in later decisions, but its precise scope varied across cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad tendency test
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech may be outlawed if it has a tendency to harm public welfare (an earlier, more permissive standard for restricting speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rooted in English common law and adopted in early U.S. cases, the bad tendency test allows punishment even without proof of imminent or likely harm. It was used in cases like Abrams, Gitlow, Frohwerk, and Debs. Criticized as ambiguous and more permissive of suppression; Holmes and Brandeis sought to replace or limit it with clearer standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imminent lawless action test (Brandenburg)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may forbid advocacy of force or law violation only 'where such advocacy is directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action' and is likely to produce such action. (Brandenburg v. Ohio, 1969).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the modern, controlling standard for speech advocating violence: it requires intent (directed to inciting), imminence (near-term), and likelihood of producing lawless action. Brandenburg substantially narrowed the circumstances where advocacy can be punished compared with earlier tests and effectively replaced the clear-and-present-danger approach for incitement cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing test: 'gravity of the evil' discounted by 'improbability' (Learned Hand / Dennis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether 'the gravity of the "evil", discounted by its improbability, justifies such invasion of free speech as is necessary to avoid the danger.' (Quoted by Chief Justice Vinson adopting Judge Learned Hand's approach in Dennis v. United States, 1951).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the seriousness of the threatened harm against how probable it is; a very grave harm can justify greater restriction even if less probable. This balancing approach was endorsed in Dennis and used mid-century in sedition/communist advocacy cases. It contrasts with stricter imminence-focused tests and can permit prevention before a putsch is 'about to be executed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Imminence requirement (Brandeis concurrence / Whitney)
rubrics_metrics.description: A more restrictive wording — 'imminent danger' — should be required before speech can be outlawed (Brandeis/Whitney concurring opinion, 1927).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concurrence urged courts to require immediacy of the danger (not merely a present tendency) before permitting punishment of speech. This emphasis on imminence influenced later doctrine culminating in Brandenburg's imminence element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness and high degree of imminence threshold (Terminiello / Bridges articulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions are permissible only when the speech is 'likely to produce a clear and present danger of a serious substantive evil that rises far above public inconvenience, annoyance, or unrest.' (Terminiello; Bridges: 'the substantive evil must be extremely serious, and the degree of imminence extremely high').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a high bar: the harm must be very serious and imminence must be high. Minor disturbances, inconvenience, or mere unrest do not justify punishment. This articulation protects robust debate and tolerates speech that provokes strong reactions unless it meets the high seriousness/imminence threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wartime context as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech restrictions may be more tolerable when the nation is at war; Holmes noted that 'When a nation is at war, many things that might be said in time of peace are such a hindrance to its effort that their utterance will not be endured so long as men fight.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the national security and military exigencies: proximity to wartime efforts and the effect on the war effort can lower the threshold for permissible restriction. Historical cases (Schenck, Frohwerk) applied this context; later jurisprudence has moderated wartime deference but still considers context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior restraint vs. punishment after the fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish advance prohibitions on speech (prior restraint) from punishment after speech occurs; prior restraints are generally more disfavored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that some restrictions are imposed in advance, and the doctrine of prior restraint is a separate, important consideration in First Amendment analysis (e.g., requiring statutes to be narrowly drawn). Courts are typically more skeptical of prior restraints than of subsequent punishment unless narrowly defined and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of unprotected or specially treated speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories of expression receive lesser or no First Amendment protection, e.g., fighting words, true threats, obscenity, speech integral to criminal conduct, and defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether speech can be restricted, identify whether the utterance falls into an established unprotected category (Chaplinsky 'fighting words', true threats, obscenity, child pornography, speech integral to criminal conduct like New York v. Ferber). These categories enable restriction without relying solely on imminence or balancing tests; case examples and citations in the article illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited applicability and historical variability of tests
rubrics_metrics.description: No single test has been uniformly applied: the clear-and-present-danger test was 'never fully adopted' as a universal rule and was superseded or modified over time (ultimately by Brandenburg's imminent lawless action test in 1969).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize doctrinal evolution and that courts have moved among tests (bad tendency, clear-and-present-danger, balancing, Brandenburg). When analyzing a case, identify the controlling precedent and the test the court applies rather than assuming one fixed standard. Historical cases (Schenck, Abrams, Gitlow, Whitney, Dennis, Brandenburg) show shifting emphases.
